title: The Startup Drake Equation: why startups fail by default and how to stack the odds
summary: Jason Cohen models startup success as a chain of "ands" where any single failing factor is fatal, so failure is the default outcome. He lays out moves to improve the odds: crush a few areas, pick the easiest market for you, build a complementary founding team, design out your weaknesses, play asymmetric games and attack the highest risks first.

principles.text: Startups fail by default because many things must all go right; one failed factor is fatal, so spend time on the biggest risks.
principles.quote: The failure of just one element is fatal, so we should spend more time identifying and then addressing the biggest areas of risk.

principles.text: Be overwhelming in one or two areas (distribution, expertise, community) so it compensates for weaknesses elsewhere.
principles.quote: You gain both focus and a higher probability of success when you have a singular winning attribute, even when you're terrible at everything else.

principles.text: Pick the market that is easiest for you to serve and profitable, not just the one that would be delighted. Big growing markets are easier.
principles.quote: What would be the *easiest* customer segment for us to target?

principles.text: Choose co-founders who zero out different risks, such as one builder and one growth marketer, rather than two of the same.
principles.quote: Two technical co-founders is far less interesting.

principles.text: Design your strategy to route around your weaknesses instead of trying to fix them; a constraint can become an advantage.
principles.quote: you can make choices that slalom around most of your weaknesses, making them irrelevant, rather than forcing you to do the impossible

principles.text: Play asymmetric games with capped downside and large upside; a few big wins can outweigh many failures.
principles.quote: Pick games where the downside is 1x but the upside potential is 10x or 100x.
